title: Sound Interference and Resonance: Standing Waves in Air Columns
lead: Sound is a wave, and so two sounds that meet add and subtract like the simple numbers their gauge pressures are. This section follows that adding twice: once into the headphones that cancel outside noise, and once into a tube, where a sound sent down the tube comes back and meets itself. Only certain frequencies come back in step, and those are the ones the air column sounds, which is why a tube closed at one end and a tube open at both ends sing different notes and why a violin and a guitar of the same note do not sound alike.
objectives: Define antinode, node, fundamental, overtones, and harmonics.
Identify instances of sound interference in everyday situations.
Describe how sound interference occurring inside open and closed tubes changes the characteristics of the sound, and how this applies to sounds produced by musical instruments.
Calculate the length of a tube using sound wave measurements.
summary_html:
• Sound interference and resonance have the same properties as defined for all waves.
  • In air columns, the lowest-frequency resonance is called the fundamental, whereas all higher resonant frequencies are called overtones. Collectively, they are called harmonics.
  • The resonant frequencies of a tube closed at one end are: $\kfn = n\frac{\kvw}{4L}\text{,}n = 1, 3, 5\text{.}\text{.}\text{.,}$ $\kfone$ is the fundamental and $L$ is the length of the tube.
  • The resonant frequencies of a tube open at both ends are: $\kfn = n\frac{\kvw}{2L}\text{,}n = 1, 2, 3\text{.}\text{.}\text{.}$

figures.original_caption: Headphones designed to cancel noise with destructive interference create a sound wave exactly opposite to the incoming sound. These headphones can be more effective than the simple passive attenuation used in most ear protection. Such headphones were used on the record-setting, around the world nonstop flight of the Voyager aircraft to protect the pilots’ hearing from engine noise.

Resonance of air in a tube closed at one end, caused by a tuning fork. (Figure 17.22) A disturbance moves down the tube. (Figure 17.23) The disturbance reflects from the closed end of the tube. (Figure 17.24) If the length of the tube L is just right, the disturbance gets back to the tuning fork half a cycle later and interferes constructively with the continuing sound from the tuning fork. This interference forms a standing wave, and the air column resonates. (Figure 17.25) A graph of air displacement along the length of the tube shows none at the closed end, where the motion is constrained, and a maximum at the open end. This standing wave has one-fourth of its wavelength in the tube, so that λ = 4L. (Figure 17.26) The same standing wave is created in the tube by a vibration introduced near its closed end.

(Figure 17.27) Another resonance for a tube closed at one end. This has maximum air displacements at the open end, and none at the closed end. The wavelength is shorter, with three-fourths λ′ equaling the length of the tube, so that λ′ = 4L/3. This higher-frequency vibration is the first overtone. (Figure 17.28) The fundamental and three lowest overtones for a tube closed at one end. All have maximum air displacements at the open end and none at the closed end. (Figure 17.30) The resonant frequencies of a tube open at both ends are shown, including the fundamental and the first three overtones. In all cases the maximum air displacements occur at both ends of the tube, giving it different natural frequencies than a tube closed at one end.

exercises.prompt: Describe how noise-canceling headphones differ from standard headphones used to block outside sounds.

answer.solution: Regular headphones only block sound waves with a physical barrier. Noise-canceling headphones use destructive interference to reduce the loudness of outside sounds.

exercises.prompt: How is it possible to use a standing wave's node and antinode to determine the length of a closed-end tube?

answer.solution: When the tube resonates at its natural frequency, the wave's node is located at the closed end of the tube, and the antinode is located at the open end. The length of the tube is equal to one-fourth of the wavelength of this wave. Thus, if we know the wavelength of the wave, we can determine the length of the tube.

exercises.prompt: A common misconception is that two wave pulses traveling in opposite directions will reflect off each other. Outline a procedure that you would use to convince someone that the two wave pulses do not reflect off each other, but instead travel through each other. You may use sketches to represent your understanding. Be sure to provide evidence to not only refute the original claim, but to support yours as well.

answer.solution: Send two pulses toward each other along a stretched spring and mark where each one started. If the pulses reflected, each would return to the side it came from, and a pulse that started on the left would never be seen on the right. Sketch the spring at three moments: before the pulses meet, while they overlap, and after. While they overlap the spring takes a single shape that is the sum of the two, and after they separate each pulse carries on with the size, shape and direction it had before, which is what a reflection cannot produce. Sound gives the same evidence: two people can talk across a room at the same time and each is heard clearly, because the sound waves pass through one another instead of bouncing off.

figure.alt: Two sinusoidal waves of the same magnitude but opposite phase with only one full period are approaching each other.

exercises.prompt:
Two wave pulses are traveling toward each other on a string, as shown below. Which of the following representations correctly shows the string as the two pulses overlap?

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

answer.solution: Where the two pulses overlap, the displacement of the string is the sum of the displacements each pulse would give on its own. The two pulses here have the same size and shape but opposite signs, so at every point one lifts the string exactly as far as the other pulls it down and the sum is zero: the string is momentarily flat. Look for the picture that shows a straight string rather than one carrying a larger or a doubled wave.

exercises.prompt: A student sends a transverse wave pulse of amplitude A along a rope attached at one end. As the pulse returns to the student, a second pulse of amplitude 3A is sent along the opposite side of the rope. What is the resulting amplitude when the two pulses interact?

options: 2A, on the side of the original wave pulse
2A, on the side of the second wave pulse
answer.hint: The two pulses are on opposite sides of the rope, so one displacement is positive where the other is negative. Add them as simple numbers and see which sign is left over.

exercises.prompt: A student would like to demonstrate destructive interference using two sound sources. Explain how the student could set up this demonstration and what restrictions they would need to place upon their sources. Be sure to consider both the layout of space and the sounds created in your explanation.

answer.solution: Drive two speakers from one signal generator so that they sound the same single frequency and stay in step with each other, and face them across an open space where there is little to reflect the sound. The two sounds must have the same frequency and nearly the same amplitude, or the maxima of one can never cancel the minima of the other. Walk slowly along a line a few meters in front of the speakers: where the path from one speaker is half a wavelength longer than the path from the other, the two arrive exactly reversed and the sound falls away almost to nothing, while halfway between those places it is loud. A low frequency makes the quiet places far enough apart to walk between comfortably, since the wavelength is then a meter or more.

exercises.prompt:
A student is shaking a flexible string attached to a wooden board in a rhythmic manner. Which of the following choices will decrease the wavelength within the rope?
  1. The student could shake her hand back and forth with greater frequency.
  2. The student could shake her hand back in forth with a greater amplitude.
  3. The student could increase the tension within the rope by stepping backwards from the board.

answer.hint: The wavelength is the wave speed divided by the frequency. Ask which of the three changes the speed of a wave on the rope, which changes the frequency, and which changes neither.

figure.alt: A rounded rectangle with two points near the top, symmetrically spaced, labeled L1 and L2.

exercises.prompt: A ripple tank has two locations (L1 and L2) that vibrate in tandem as shown below. Both L1 and L2 vibrate in a plane perpendicular to the page, creating a two-dimensional interference pattern. Describe an experimental procedure to determine the speed of the waves created within the water, including all additional equipment that you would need. You may use the diagram below to help your description, or you may create one of your own. Include enough detail so that another student could carry out your experiment.

answer.solution: You need a meter rule, a stopwatch and the frequency at which the two sources are driven, which the signal generator reads out. Set the sources going at a known frequency and let the pattern settle. Lay the rule across the tank and measure the distance from one crest to the crest several wavelengths away, then divide by the number of wavelengths you counted; measuring across many wavelengths rather than one keeps the error small. The wave speed is then the frequency multiplied by that wavelength. Repeat at three or four frequencies: the wavelength should shrink as the frequency rises while the product stays the same, which is the check that you have the speed of the waves and not a mistake in the counting.

figure.alt: The figure shows a standing wave with one full wavelength on a string vibrating between two posts.

exercises.prompt: A string is vibrating between two posts as shown above. Students are to determine the speed of the wave within this string. They have already measured the amount of time necessary for the wave to oscillate up and down. The students must also take what other measurements to determine the speed of the wave?

options: The distance between the two posts.
The amplitude of the wave and the tension in the string
The distance between the two posts, the amplitude of the wave, and the tension in the string
answer.hint: The speed is the wavelength divided by the period, and the period they already have. Count how many wavelengths the picture fits between the posts.

exercises.prompt:
The accepted speed of sound in room temperature air is 346 m/s. Knowing that their school is colder than usual, a group of students is asked to determine the speed of sound in their room. They are permitted to use any materials necessary; however, their lab procedure must utilize standing wave patterns. The students collect the information below.
Trial NumberWavelength (m)Frequency (Hz)
13.4595
22.32135
31.70190
41.45240
51.08305
(a) Describe an experimental procedure the group of students could have used to obtain this data. Include diagrams of the experimental setup and any equipment used in the process.
(b) Select a set of data points from the table and plot those points on a graph to determine the speed of sound within the classroom. Fill in the blank column in the table for any quantities you graph other than the given data. Label the axes and indicate the scale for each.
(c) Using information from the graph, determine the speed of sound within the student's classroom, and explain what characteristic of the graph provides this evidence.
(d) Determine the temperature of the classroom.

answer.solution: (a) Hold a tuning fork of known frequency over a tube closed at one end whose air column can be lengthened, such as a tube standing in water that is slowly raised out of it, and listen for the length at which the sound suddenly swells. That length is one-fourth of the wavelength, so the wavelength is four times it; repeat with tuning forks of several frequencies. (b) The wavelength and the frequency are not proportional, but the wavelength and 1/f are, so fill the blank column with 1/f in seconds and plot the wavelength against it. (c) The points lie on a straight line through the origin whose slope is the speed of sound, because the wave relation is that the wavelength equals the speed times 1/f. Trials 1 and 5 give (3.45 m − 1.08 m)/(1/95 s − 1/305 s) = 328 m/s, and the other trials agree with that to within a few meters per second. (d) The speed of sound in air is (331 m/s) times the square root of T/273 K, so T = (328/331) squared times 273 K = 268 K, about −5 °C, which is indeed a cold classroom.

exercises.prompt: A tube is open at one end. If the fundamental frequency f is created by a wavelength λ, then which of the following describes the frequency and wavelength associated with the tube's fourth overtone?

answer.hint: A tube closed at one end sounds only the odd harmonics, so count them: the fundamental, the first overtone, the second, the third, the fourth. Then remember that the wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency.

exercises.prompt:
A group of students were tasked with collecting information about standing waves. The table below shows a series of their data, showing the length of an air column and a resonant frequency present when the column is struck.
Length (m)Resonant Frequency (Hz)
185.75
243
329
421.5
(a) From their data, determine whether the air column was open or closed on each end.
(b) Predict the resonant frequency of the column at a length of 2.5 meters.

answer.solution: (a) The frequency times the length is the same for every row: 85.75 Hz × 1 m = 85.75 m/s, 43 Hz × 2 m = 86 m/s, and so on. For a tube open at both ends the fundamental is v/2L, so the product would be v/2, giving v = 172 m/s; for a tube closed at one end it is v/4L, giving v = 343 m/s. Only the second is the speed of sound in air, so the column was closed at one end. (b) The product holds, so f = 85.75 m/s ÷ 2.5 m = 34.3 Hz.

exercises.prompt:
When a student blows across a glass half-full of water, a resonant frequency is created within the air column remaining in the glass. Which of the following can the student do to increase this resonant frequency?
  1. Add more water to the glass.
  2. Replace the water with a more dense fluid.
  3. Increase the temperature of the room.

answer.hint: The resonant frequency is the speed of sound in the air column divided by four times its length. Ask which of the three shortens the air column and which changes the speed of sound in air.

exercises.prompt: A student decides to test the speed of sound through wood using a wooden ruler. The student rests the ruler on a desk with half of its length protruding off the desk edge. The student then holds one end in place and strikes the protruding end with his other hand, creating a musical sound, and counts the number of vibrations of the ruler. Explain why the student would not be able to measure the speed of sound through wood using this method.

answer.solution: Striking the end of a protruding ruler would create transverse waves, not sound waves. Any measurable, audible sound would come from the repetitive striking of the ruler against the desk. The student is confused about the speed of sound through solids versus the speed of sound in air.

exercises.prompt:
A musician stands outside in a field and plucks a string on an acoustic guitar. Standing waves will most likely occur in which of the following media? Select two answers.
  1. The guitar string
  2. The air inside the guitar
  3. The air surrounding the guitar
  4. The ground beneath the musician

figure.alt: Two tubes of slightly different length are oriented parallel to each other, with the smaller one on top. Their open ends are pointed toward a speaker that is hooked up to a power source.

exercises.prompt: This figure shows two tubes that are identical except for their slightly different lengths. Both tubes have one open end and one closed end. A speaker connected to a variable frequency generator is placed in front of the tubes, as shown. The speaker is set to produce a note of very low frequency when turned on. The frequency is then slowly increased to produce resonances in the tubes. Students observe that at first only one of the tubes resonates at a time. Later, as the frequency gets very high, there are times when both tubes resonate. In a clear, coherent, paragraph-length answer, explain why there are some high frequencies, but no low frequencies, at which both tubes resonate. You may include diagrams and/or equations as part of your explanation.

answer.solution: Each tube is closed at one end, so it resonates at the odd multiples of its own fundamental, and because the two tubes have different lengths they have different fundamentals and so two different ladders of resonances. Both tubes resonate together only where a rung of one ladder falls close enough to a rung of the other that a single frequency can drive them both, and how close is close enough is set by how sharp a resonance is, which is a fixed fraction of the frequency rather than a fixed number of hertz. Low down, the rungs of the two ladders are far apart in hertz compared with that width, because the two fundamentals differ by a good fraction of themselves, so no low frequency lies near a resonance of both tubes. As the frequency rises, each tube's rungs grow in size and so does the width of each resonance, while the two ladders drift in and out of step with each other, and sooner or later a high harmonic of the short tube lands within the width of a high harmonic of the long one. At those frequencies, and only those, both tubes sound at once.

figure.alt: An oscillator is set on a table that has a pulley on one end. This oscillator is connected by a string through the pulley to a mass. There are arrows on the connection between the pulley and string to indicate that the oscillator is moving the string.

exercises.prompt: A student connects one end of a string with negligible mass to an oscillator. The other end of the string is passed over a pulley and attached to a suspended weight, as shown above. The student finds that a standing wave with one antinode is formed on the string when the frequency of the oscillator is f0. The student then moves the oscillator to shorten the horizontal segment of string to half its original length. At what frequency will a standing wave with one antinode now be formed on the string?

options: There is no frequency at which a standing wave will be formed.
answer.hint: The tension and the string are unchanged, so the wave travels at the same speed. Halving the length halves the wavelength of the pattern with one antinode.

exercises.prompt:
A guitar string of length L is bound at both ends. The table below shows the string's harmonic frequencies when struck.
Harmonic NumberFrequency
1225/L
2450/L
3675/L
4900/L
(a) Based on the information above, what is the speed of the wave within the string?
(b) The guitarist then slides her finger along the neck of the guitar, changing the string length as a result. Calculate the fundamental frequency of the string and wave speed present if the string length is reduced to 2/3 L.

answer.solution: (a) A string bound at both ends has its fundamental at v/2L, and the table gives that fundamental as 225/L, so v/2L = 225/L and the wave speed is 450 m/s. (b) The tension and the string itself are unchanged, so the wave speed is still 450 m/s. The new length is 2L/3, and the fundamental is v divided by twice that length: 450 ÷ (4L/3) = 337.5/L, which is 1.5 times the old fundamental.

exercises.prompt: How does an unamplified guitar produce sounds so much more intense than those of a plucked string held taut by a simple stick?

answer.solution: A plucked string is thin, and it can push very little air aside as it moves, so almost all of its energy stays in the string. The guitar couples the string through the bridge to the sounding box and to the air inside it, which resonates with the string's frequencies. The large face of the box and the air in it move a great deal of air, and the same energy in the string is therefore carried away as sound far more quickly than a bare string could carry it. A stick makes no such coupling, so the note it holds is faint.

exercises.prompt: You are given two wind instruments of identical length. One is open at both ends, whereas the other is closed at one end. Which is able to produce the lowest frequency?

answer.solution: The instrument closed at one end. Its fundamental holds one-fourth of a wavelength in the tube, so the wavelength is four times the length and the frequency is the speed of sound divided by four times the length. The instrument open at both ends holds half a wavelength, so its fundamental is the speed of sound divided by twice the length, which is twice as high. For the same length, then, the closed tube sounds an octave lower.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between an overtone and a harmonic? Are all harmonics overtones? Are all overtones harmonics?

answer.solution: An overtone is any resonant frequency above the fundamental, while the harmonics are the fundamental and its overtones taken together, numbered by the multiple of the fundamental they stand at. So every overtone is a harmonic, but not every harmonic is an overtone: the fundamental is the first harmonic and is not an overtone at all. The numbering therefore runs one step apart, and for a tube closed at one end it runs further apart still, since only the odd harmonics are present and the first overtone is the third harmonic.

exercises.prompt: A “showy” custom-built car has two brass horns that are supposed to produce the same frequency but actually emit 263.8 and 264.5 Hz. What beat frequency is produced?

answer.solution: 0.7 Hz

exercises.prompt: What beat frequencies result if a piano hammer hits three strings that emit frequencies of 127.8, 128.1, and 128.3 Hz?
(a) What is the fundamental frequency of a 0.672-m-long tube, open at both ends, on a day when the speed of sound is 344 m/s? (b) What is the frequency of its second harmonic?

What are the first three overtones of a bassoon that has a fundamental frequency of 90.0 Hz? It is open at both ends. (The overtones of a real bassoon are more complex than this example, because its double reed makes it act more like a tube closed at one end.)
What length should an oboe have to produce a fundamental frequency of 110 Hz on a day when the speed of sound is 343 m/s? It is open at both ends.

(a) Find the length of an organ pipe closed at one end that produces a fundamental frequency of 256 Hz when air temperature is $18.0^\circ\text{C}$. (b) What is its fundamental frequency at $25.0^\circ\text{C}$?

The ear canal resonates like a tube closed at one end. (See Figure 17.37.) If ear canals range in length from 1.80 to 2.60 cm in an average population, what is the range of fundamental resonant frequencies? Take air temperature to be $37.0^\circ\text{C}$, which is the same as body temperature. How does this result correlate with the intensity versus frequency graph (Figure 17.35) of the human ear?

A crude approximation of voice production is to consider the breathing passages and mouth to be a resonating tube closed at one end. (See Figure 17.29.) (a) What is the fundamental frequency if the tube is 0.240-m long, by taking air temperature to be $37.0^\circ\text{C}$? (b) What would this frequency become if the person replaced the air with helium? Assume the same temperature dependence for helium as for air.
What frequencies will a 1.80-m-long tube produce in the audible range at $20.0^\circ\text{C}$ if: (a) The tube is closed at one end? (b) It is open at both ends?
